module.title: Future Plans & Intentions with 'Be Going To'
module.objective: Express predetermined future plans and personal intentions accurately using the 'be going to + verb' structure.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Our Future Plans & Dreams
subModules.grammarFocus: Be Going To + Verb (Affirmative, Negative, and Question Forms)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Future time expressions, common verbs for plans and intentions

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission! In this lesson, you are going to read a fun passage about friends talking about their future plans. You will learn how to understand sentences with 'be going to + verb' — the structure we use when we already have a plan or intention for the future. By the end of this mission, you will be able to spot future plans in a text, understand who is going to do what, and answer questions about the details. Let's get started!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Recognizing and understanding 'be going to + base verb' in affirmative, negative, and question forms within a reading passage.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Future time expressions (tomorrow, tonight, next week, next month, next year) and common action verbs (visit, study, travel, buy, cook, meet, move, start).
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the passage first to understand the main idea (What is the text about?), then scanning for specific details (Who is going to do what? When?).

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about people's future plans and intentions.
Identify key details including who is going to do each activity and when they plan to do it.
Recognize the 'be going to + verb' structure in affirmative, negative, and question sentences within the passage.
Distinguish between plans that are confirmed and plans that are not happening (negative form).

contextWarmup.prompt: Your friend says: 'I am going to visit my grandmother this weekend.' What does this sentence tell you?
options: Your friend already has a plan to visit grandmother this weekend.
Your friend visited grandmother last weekend.
Your friend visits grandmother every weekend.
contextWarmup.explanation: Great! 'I am going to visit' tells us about a future plan that is already decided. The words 'this weekend' tell us when. It is not about the past or a regular habit — it is a specific plan for the future!

rules: When you see 'am/is/are + going to + verb' in a text, it tells you about a future plan or intention that someone has already decided.
Look for time expressions like 'tomorrow,' 'tonight,' 'next week,' or 'next month' — they often appear near 'be going to' sentences and help you understand WHEN the plan will happen.
In negative sentences ('is not going to' or 'isn't going to'), the person has decided NOT to do something. Pay attention to 'not' — it changes the whole meaning!
In questions ('Are you going to...?'), someone is asking about another person's plan. Look for the answer (Yes, I am / No, I'm not) to understand the plan.

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners confuse 'going to + verb' (a future plan) with 'going to + place' (traveling somewhere right now). When you read a sentence, check: Is there a BASE VERB after 'going to'? If yes, it is a future plan. If there is a place name, it might mean someone is traveling there now.
commonTrap.wrong: Reading 'She is going to cook dinner' and thinking she is walking to a place called 'cook dinner.'
commonTrap.correct: Understanding that 'She is going to cook dinner' means she has a plan to cook dinner in the future.

sections.title: Reading Passage: A Busy Weekend Ahead

content.context: Three friends — Rina, Tom, and Maya — are chatting at school on Friday afternoon. They are talking about their plans for the weekend.
content.text:
It is Friday afternoon. Rina, Tom, and Maya are talking about their weekend plans.

Rina says, "I'm going to visit my grandmother tomorrow. She lives in a small town near the mountains. I'm going to cook lunch for her. I'm very excited!"

Tom smiles and says, "That sounds nice, Rina! I'm going to study for my English test on Monday. I'm not going to play video games this weekend. I really need to focus."

Maya laughs and says, "You are so serious, Tom! I'm going to meet my cousins at the park on Saturday. We're going to have a picnic. On Sunday, I'm going to prepare my bag for school."

Rina asks Tom, "Are you going to study all day?" Tom replies, "No, I'm not. I'm going to take a break in the evening. Maybe I'm going to watch a movie."

"That's a good plan!" says Maya. "We are all going to have a great weekend!"

highlights.note: Affirmative form: Subject + am + going to + base verb (visit). Rina has already decided to visit her grandmother.
Another affirmative example: Rina plans to cook lunch. Notice 'cook' is in the base form.
Negative form: Subject + am + not + going to + base verb. Tom decided NOT to play video games.
Question form: Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + base verb? Rina is asking about Tom's plan.
An adjective that means feeling very happy and enthusiastic about something.
A meal that you eat outside, often in a park. A fun weekend activity!
A common expression meaning to stop working and rest for a short time.
To make something ready. Maya is going to prepare her bag for school on Sunday.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Three friends talking about their plans for the weekend.
Three friends remembering what they did last weekend.
Three friends studying English together at school.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage is about Rina, Tom, and Maya sharing their future plans for the weekend. They use 'be going to' to talk about what they will do on Saturday and Sunday. It is not about the past or about studying together.

detailQuestions.prompt: What is Rina going to do tomorrow?
options: She is going to visit her grandmother and cook lunch for her.
She is going to meet her cousins at the park.
She is going to study for her English test.
detailQuestions.explanation: Rina says, 'I'm going to visit my grandmother tomorrow' and 'I'm going to cook lunch for her.' These are Rina's two plans. Meeting cousins is Maya's plan, and studying is Tom's plan.

detailQuestions.prompt: What is Tom NOT going to do this weekend?
options: He is not going to play video games.
He is not going to study for his test.
He is not going to watch a movie.
detailQuestions.explanation: Tom clearly says, 'I'm not going to play video games this weekend.' He IS going to study, and he mentions he might watch a movie in the evening. The negative form 'not going to' tells us what he decided against doing.

detailQuestions.prompt: What is Maya going to do on Sunday?
options: She is going to prepare her bag for school.
She is going to have a picnic with her cousins.
She is going to visit her grandmother.
detailQuestions.explanation: Maya says, 'On Sunday, I'm going to prepare my bag for school.' The picnic with her cousins is on Saturday, not Sunday. Visiting grandmother is Rina's plan, not Maya's.

questions.question: According to the passage, where does Rina's grandmother live?
options: In a small town near the mountains.
In a big city near the beach.
In the same town as Rina.
questions.answer: In a small town near the mountains.
questions.explanation: Rina says, 'She lives in a small town near the mountains.' This detail is stated directly in the passage. Always scan the text for specific location words!

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses the NEGATIVE form of 'be going to'?
options: I'm not going to play video games this weekend.
I'm going to study for my English test.
We're going to have a picnic.
questions.answer: I'm not going to play video games this weekend.
questions.explanation: The negative form uses 'not' between 'am/is/are' and 'going to.' Tom says 'I'm not going to play video games,' which shows a decision NOT to do something. The other two sentences are affirmative (positive) plans.

questions.question: When Rina asks, 'Are you going to study all day?' — what does Tom answer?
options: No, I'm not. He is going to take a break in the evening.
Yes, I am. He is going to study all day and all night.
He doesn't answer the question.
questions.answer: No, I'm not. He is going to take a break in the evening.
questions.explanation: Tom replies, 'No, I'm not. I'm going to take a break in the evening.' This shows how to answer a 'be going to' question with a short negative answer and then give more details about the plan.

questions.question: Read this sentence: 'We're going to have a picnic.' Who says this in the passage?
options: Maya, talking about her plan with her cousins.
Rina, talking about her plan with her grandmother.
Tom, talking about his plan with his friends.
questions.answer: Maya, talking about her plan with her cousins.
questions.explanation: Maya says, 'I'm going to meet my cousins at the park on Saturday. We're going to have a picnic.' The word 'we' refers to Maya and her cousins. Scanning for who is speaking helps you understand the details!

questions.question: Which of these is the correct structure for 'be going to' in a question?
options: Are you going to study tonight?
You are going to study tonight?
Going to are you study tonight?
questions.answer: Are you going to study tonight?
questions.explanation: To form a question with 'be going to,' we move the 'be' verb (am/is/are) to the front: 'Are + you + going to + study + tonight?' This is the correct word order for yes/no questions.

questions.question: At the end of the passage, Maya says, 'We are all going to have a great weekend!' What does this sentence express?
options: A positive feeling about everyone's future plans.
A question about what everyone did last weekend.
A complaint that the weekend is too busy.
questions.answer: A positive feeling about everyone's future plans.
questions.explanation: Maya uses 'be going to' to express a happy, confident feeling about the future. The word 'great' shows it is positive. She is not asking a question or complaining — she is sharing her excitement about everyone's plans!

questions.question: Look at this sentence from the passage: 'I'm going to cook lunch for her.' What form is the verb 'cook' in?
options: Base form (infinitive) — the simple, unchanged form of the verb.
Past tense — the verb shows a completed action.
Present continuous (-ing form) — the verb shows an action happening now.
questions.answer: Base form (infinitive) — the simple, unchanged form of the verb.
questions.explanation: After 'going to,' we always use the base form of the verb. 'Cook' is the base form. We do NOT say 'going to cooks,' 'going to cooked,' or 'going to cooking.' This is an important rule to remember!

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Weekend Plans with 'Be Going To'

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear two school friends, Sarah and Tom, talking about their weekend plans in the school canteen. They use the structure 'be going to + verb' to share their future plans and intentions. Your goal is to listen carefully for key phrases like 'I'm going to...', 'Are you going to...?', and 'She's going to...' to understand what each person plans to do. Pay attention to the subject (I, you, she, he) and the main verb after 'going to' to catch the specific activity each speaker mentions.
learningObjectives: Identify future plans and intentions when speakers use 'be going to + verb' in natural spoken English.
Distinguish between affirmative, negative, and question forms of 'be going to' in spoken dialogue.
Recognise time expressions such as 'tomorrow', 'this weekend', and 'next week' that signal future plans.
Understand connected speech patterns where 'going to' is reduced to 'gonna' in fast, natural conversation.

keyPhrases.note: Used to talk about a plan you have already decided. The verb 'visit' comes after 'going to'.
This is the question form. 'Are' moves to the front of the sentence to make a yes/no question.
Used to describe someone else's plan. 'She's' is the contraction of 'She is'.
The negative form. Add 'not' after 'am/is/are' to say you do NOT plan to do something.

keyPhrases.phrase: What are you going to do?
keyPhrases.note: A common question to ask about someone's future plans. 'What' is the question word, followed by 'are you going to do'.

keyPhrases.phrase: I'm going to help my dad
keyPhrases.note: Another example of a decided plan using 'be going to' followed by the base verb 'help'.

connectedSpeech.note: In fast speech, 'going to' is almost always reduced to 'gonna'. The words blend together so 'going to' sounds like one word: 'gonna'. This is very common and completely natural.

connectedSpeech.slow: What are you going to do?
connectedSpeech.note: 'What are you' blends into 'whaddya' and 'going to' becomes 'gonna'. This is a very common fast-speech pattern in everyday English questions about plans.
'She is' contracts to 'she's' and 'going to' reduces to 'gonna'. Listen for the 'z' sound at the end of 'she's' linking into 'gonna'.
'You' weakens to 'ya' in fast speech, and 'going to' becomes 'gonna'. The rising intonation at the end tells you it is a question.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: My Future Plans with 'Be Going To'

content.summary: In this writing blueprint, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about your future plans and intentions. We use 'be going to + verb' when we talk about things we already decided to do. You will practice writing positive sentences, negative sentences, and questions about the future. Follow each step carefully and pay attention to spelling, capitals, and punctuation.

blueprintItems.title: Write a Positive Future Plan
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + am/is/are + going to + verb (base form) + extra info.
blueprintItems.example: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.

blueprintItems.title: Write a Negative Future Plan
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + am/is/are + not + going to + verb (base form) + extra info.
blueprintItems.example: She is not going to buy that dress.

blueprintItems.title: Write a Yes/No Question about Future Plans
blueprintItems.formula: Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + verb (base form) + extra info?
blueprintItems.example: Are you going to study tonight?

blueprintItems.title: Write a Short Answer to a Future Plan Question
blueprintItems.formula: Yes, + subject + am/is/are. / No, + subject + am/is/are + not.
blueprintItems.example: Yes, I am. / No, I am not.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start your sentence with a capital letter and end with a period (.) for statements or a question mark (?) for questions.
mechanicsRules.badExample: she is going to cook dinner tonight
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She is going to cook dinner tonight.
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence must begin with a capital letter. Statements end with a period, and questions end with a question mark.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'am' with 'I', use 'is' with 'he/she/it', and use 'are' with 'you/we/they'. Do not mix them up.
mechanicsRules.badExample: I is going to travel next week.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I am going to travel next week.
mechanicsRules.why: The verb 'be' must agree with the subject. 'I' always takes 'am', 'he/she/it' takes 'is', and 'you/we/they' take 'are'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always write 'going to' before the base form of the verb. Do not add '-ing' or '-s' to the main verb after 'going to'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He is going to plays football.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He is going to play football.
mechanicsRules.why: After 'going to', the main verb must stay in its base form (infinitive). We do not change it.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place 'not' between 'am/is/are' and 'going to' for negative sentences. You can also use contractions: isn't, aren't.
mechanicsRules.badExample: They going to not watch the movie.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: They are not going to watch the movie.
mechanicsRules.why: In negative sentences with 'be going to', the word 'not' comes right after 'am', 'is', or 'are'.

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 1: My Plans for This Weekend
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short paragraph (3 to 5 sentences) about your plans for this weekend. Use 'be going to' in every sentence. Include at least one positive sentence, one negative sentence, and one question to a friend. Use time words like 'on Saturday', 'on Sunday', or 'this weekend'.
guidedLabChallenges.example: I am going to visit my cousin on Saturday. We are going to play football in the park. I am not going to stay home all day. Are you going to come with us on Sunday?
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Start writing your weekend plans here...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 2: My Friend's Future Plans
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Imagine your best friend told you about his or her plans for next month. Write a short paragraph (3 to 5 sentences) describing your friend's plans. Use 'is going to' or 'is not going to' with he or she. Include at least one thing your friend is going to do and one thing your friend is not going to do.
guidedLabChallenges.example: My friend Rina is going to start a dance class next month. She is going to practice every Wednesday. She is not going to miss any class. She is going to perform at the school festival in December.
guidedLabChallenges.placeholder: Start writing about your friend's plans here...

guidedLabChallenges.title: Challenge 3: Our Holiday Plans
guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) about your family's or your group's holiday plans. Use 'we are going to' and 'we are not going to'. Add time words like 'next holiday', 'next year', or 'in July'. Try to include a question sentence asking a family member or friend about their plans.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write three sentences about what you are going to do after school today. Use 'am going to' in each sentence. Include a time word in at least one sentence.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Each sentence uses 'I am going to + base verb' correctly. At least one sentence has a time expression (e.g., 'today', 'tonight', 'this afternoon'). All sentences start with a capital letter and end with a period. Spelling of common words is correct.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: I am going to eat lunch with my friends today. I am going to do my homework at home. I am going to read a book tonight.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write two negative sentences and one question about future plans. Use 'is not going to' or 'are not going to' for the negative sentences. Use 'Is' or 'Are' to start the question.
practicumQuestions.criteria: Negative sentences correctly use 'subject + is/are + not + going to + base verb'. The question uses correct word order: 'Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + base verb?' All sentences have correct capitalization and punctuation. The main verb after 'going to' is in base form.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) about your plans for next year. Include at least two positive sentences with 'going to', one negative sentence with 'not going to', and one question. Use different subjects (I, he, she, we, they).
practicumQuestions.criteria: The paragraph has 4 to 6 sentences. It includes at least two positive 'be going to' sentences, one negative 'be going to' sentence, and one question with 'be going to'. Different subjects are used (not only 'I'). Correct subject-verb agreement with am/is/are. All sentences have proper capitalization and end punctuation. Time expressions related to the future are present.
practicumQuestions.sampleGoodAnswer: Next year, I am going to learn how to swim. My sister is going to start university. We are going to move to a new house. My brother is not going to change his school. Are they going to visit us next summer? I am going to work very hard.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Talking About Your Future Plans with 'Be Going To'

content.summary: In this speaking lab, you will practise talking about your future plans and intentions using 'be going to + verb'. At the A1 level, it is very important to say 'going to' clearly and with the correct rhythm. In natural spoken English, 'going to' is often reduced to 'gonna' in casual speech, but for clear A1 practice, we will say the full form 'going to'. You will learn how to stress the main verb after 'going to', use falling intonation for statements about plans, and use rising intonation for yes/no questions about plans. Listen carefully to the rhythm: 'I'm GOING to VISIT my uncle.' The stress falls on 'GOING' and the main verb 'VISIT'. Keep your sentences short and clear.
content.audioGuidance: When you say 'I'm going to travel by train', make sure you pronounce 'going' as /ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ/ with a clear /ŋ/ sound at the end — do not drop the 'g'. The word 'to' before the verb is usually weak: /tə/. So the natural rhythm is: 'I'm GOing tə TRAvel by TRAIN.' For yes/no questions like 'Are you going to stay?', your voice should rise at the end. For statements like 'I'm going to visit museums', your voice should fall at the end. Practise saying each sentence slowly first, then at normal speed.

pillars.name: Stress on Content Words
pillars.target: Emphasise verbs and nouns in 'be going to' sentences
pillars.explanation: In a sentence like 'I'm going to visit my uncle', the most important words are 'GOING', 'VISIT', and 'UNCLE'. These content words should be louder and clearer than small words like 'I'm', 'to', and 'my'. This helps your listener understand your plan easily.

pillars.name: Falling Intonation for Plans
pillars.target: Use falling tone when stating future plans
pillars.explanation: When you tell someone your plan, your voice goes down at the end. For example: 'I'm going to travel by train.' ↘ This falling intonation shows that you are making a clear statement, not asking a question.

pillars.name: Rising Intonation for Yes/No Questions
pillars.target: Use rising tone for questions about plans
pillars.explanation: When you ask a yes/no question about someone's plans, your voice goes up at the end. For example: 'Are you going to stay for a long time?' ↗ This rising intonation tells the listener that you expect a 'yes' or 'no' answer.

pillars.name: Linking and Weak Forms
pillars.target: Connect words smoothly in 'going to' phrases
pillars.explanation: In natural speech, 'going to' links together smoothly. The word 'to' becomes weak /tə/. Practise saying 'going-tə-visit' as one smooth phrase without pausing between each word. This makes your English sound more natural and fluent.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: When 'visit' stands alone, stress is on 'VIS'. In the phrase 'going to visit', there are two stress points: 'GO' and 'VIS'. The word 'to' stays weak and unstressed. This creates a nice rhythm: STRONG-weak-weak-STRONG-weak.

The word 'travel' keeps its stress on 'TRAV' when placed in the phrase 'going to travel'. Notice how 'GO' also carries stress. The rhythm pattern is the same: STRONG-weak-weak-STRONG-weak. This regular beat makes your speech clear.
The word 'museum' has stress on the second syllable 'SE'. In the longer phrase 'visit a museum', both 'VIS' and 'SE' carry stress. The small word 'a' is very weak. Practise: VIS-it-a-mu-SE-um.
The word 'holiday' always keeps its stress on 'HOL', the first syllable. When we add 'on' before it, 'on' stays weak and unstressed. The rhythm is: weak-STRONG-weak-weak.

drills.targetText: I'm going to visit my uncle.
drills.hint: Say 'going' with a clear /ŋ/ sound. Keep 'to' short and weak like /tə/. Make 'visit' and 'uncle' louder than the other words.

drills.targetText: I'm going to travel by train.
drills.focus: Linking 'going to' smoothly and stressing 'travel' and 'train'
drills.hint: Link 'going' and 'to' together: 'going-tə'. Make sure 'train' rhymes with 'rain'. The /tr/ at the start of 'train' and 'travel' should be clear.

drills.targetText: Are you going to stay for a long time?
drills.phonetic: /ɑːr juː ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈsteɪ fɔːr ə ˈlɒŋ ˈtaɪm/
drills.hint: Start the question at a normal pitch. Let your voice rise on the last word 'time'. This rising tone shows it is a yes/no question.

drills.targetText: I'm going to visit some museums.
drills.focus: Pronouncing 'museums' with correct stress on second syllable
drills.hint: The word 'museums' has stress on 'ZE': mu-ZE-ums. Do not say 'MU-se-ums'. Also, the 's' at the end is voiced: /z/.

drills.targetText: I'm not going to stay for a long time.
drills.phonetic: /aɪm ˈnɒt ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈsteɪ fɔːr ə ˈlɒŋ ˈtaɪm/
drills.hint: Stress the word 'NOT' clearly to show the negative. Your voice should fall at the end of this statement because you are giving information, not asking a question.

drills.targetText: What are you going to do next weekend?
drills.phonetic: /wɒt ɑːr juː ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈduː nɛkst ˈwiːk.ɛnd/
drills.hint: WH-questions (what, where, when) use falling intonation. Your voice should go down on 'weekend'. Stress 'WHAT', 'GOING', 'DO', and 'WEEKEND'.

roleplay.context: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul about your holiday plans next week. Mr. Khoirul is your friendly English teacher. He wants to know about your future plans. You must answer his questions using 'be going to + verb'. Speak clearly and use falling intonation for your statements.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! I heard you have a holiday next week. What are you going to do?
turns.translation: Halo! Saya dengar kamu punya liburan minggu depan. Apa yang akan kamu lakukan?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm going to visit my uncle in Surabaya.
turns.translation: Saya akan mengunjungi paman saya di Surabaya.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That sounds wonderful! How are you going to travel there?
turns.translation: Kedengarannya luar biasa! Bagaimana kamu akan pergi ke sana?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm going to travel by train with my family.
turns.translation: Saya akan naik kereta bersama keluarga saya.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Nice! Are you going to stay there for a long time?
turns.translation: Bagus! Apakah kamu akan tinggal di sana untuk waktu yang lama?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: No, I'm not. I'm going to stay for three days only.
turns.translation: Tidak. Saya akan tinggal selama tiga hari saja.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Great! What are you going to do in Surabaya?
turns.translation: Bagus! Apa yang akan kamu lakukan di Surabaya?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I'm going to visit some museums and try the local food.
turns.translation: Saya akan mengunjungi beberapa museum dan mencoba makanan lokal.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your plans for next weekend. Use 'be going to' for each plan. Follow the three story points below. Speak clearly with falling intonation for each statement.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me about your plans for next weekend. What are you going to do? Where are you going to go? Who are you going to be with? Use 'I'm going to' in your story.
storyPoints: Say where you are going to go next weekend and why.
Say what activity you are going to do there.
Say who you are going to go with and how you are going to travel.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Next weekend, I'm going to go to the beach because I love the sea. I'm going to swim and play in the sand. I'm going to go with my friends, and we are going to travel by car.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /nɛkst ˈwiːk.ɛnd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ tə ðə biːtʃ bɪˈkɒz aɪ lʌv ðə siː. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə swɪm ænd pleɪ ɪn ðə sænd. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ wɪð maɪ frɛndz ænd wiː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈtræv.əl baɪ kɑːr/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to use 'I'm going to' before each verb. Speak slowly and clearly. Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using 'be going to' to describe future plans in a connected monologue. You should use the structure 'subject + be going to + base verb' for each plan. Falling intonation at the end of each statement shows confidence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about your plans for the school holiday. Use 'be going to' to describe three different plans. Follow the story points below and speak with clear pronunciation.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please tell me about your school holiday plans. What are you going to do during the holiday? Tell me about three things you are going to do. Use 'I'm going to' or 'We are going to' in your story.
storyPoints: Say what you are going to do in the first week of the holiday.
Say what food you are going to try or cook.
Say what you are NOT going to do during the holiday and why.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: In the first week, I'm going to visit my grandparents in the village. I'm going to try my grandmother's special fried rice. I'm not going to study every day because I want to relax and have fun.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪn ðə fɜːrst wiːk aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈvɪz.ɪt maɪ ˈɡrænd.pɛr.ənts ɪn ðə ˈvɪl.ɪdʒ. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə traɪ maɪ ˈɡrænd.mʌð.ərz ˈspɛʃ.əl fraɪd raɪs. aɪm nɒt ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈstʌd.i ˈɛv.ri deɪ bɪˈkɒz aɪ wɒnt tə rɪˈlæks ænd hæv fʌn/
practicumQuestions.hint: Include one negative sentence using 'I'm NOT going to'. Stress the word 'NOT' clearly. Remember to follow all three story points.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises both affirmative and negative forms of 'be going to'. Using 'I'm not going to' is important for expressing things you do not plan to do. The three story points guide you to create a structured monologue.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are calling your friend to talk about your plans for tomorrow. Your friend will ask you questions about your plans. Answer using 'I'm going to + verb'. Be friendly and speak clearly.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is your friend calling. I want to know about your plans for tomorrow. Let's talk about what you are going to do!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are having a phone call with your friend. Tomorrow is Saturday and you have no school. Your friend wants to know your plans. You have planned to go shopping at the mall, eat lunch at a restaurant, and watch a movie in the evening. Use 'I'm going to' to tell your friend about each plan.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student talking to your friend on the phone. You are excited about your plans for tomorrow. You should answer questions about where you are going to go, what you are going to eat, and what you are going to do in the evening.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I'm going to go shopping at the mall. Then I'm going to eat lunch at a restaurant. In the evening, I'm going to watch a movie.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ ˈʃɒp.ɪŋ æt ðə mɔːl. ðɛn aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə iːt lʌntʃ æt ə ˈrɛs.tər.ɒnt. ɪn ðə ˈiːv.nɪŋ aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə wɒtʃ ə ˈmuː.vi/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use time words like 'then' and 'in the evening' to organise your plans. Speak with enthusiasm because you are excited about tomorrow!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'be going to' in a natural phone conversation. You need to respond to your friend's questions with clear plans using the target structure. Using time markers helps organise your ideas.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, about your plans after you finish school today. He will ask you several questions. Answer each question using 'be going to'.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good afternoon! Before you go home today, I want to ask you about your plans for this afternoon and evening. What are you going to do after school?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are in the classroom after the last lesson. Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, wants to practise English conversation with you. He asks about your plans for this afternoon. You plan to go home, do your homework, help your mother cook dinner, and then read a book before bed.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student speaking to your English teacher Mr. Khoirul. You should be polite and answer in complete sentences using 'I'm going to'. You are a responsible student who has clear plans for the afternoon.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: After school, I'm going to go home and do my homework. Then I'm going to help my mother cook dinner. Before bed, I'm going to read a book.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈæf.tər skuːl aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ hoʊm ænd duː maɪ ˈhoʊm.wɜːrk. ðɛn aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə hɛlp maɪ ˈmʌð.ər kʊk ˈdɪn.ər. bɪˈfɔːr bɛd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə riːd ə bʊk/
practicumQuestions.hint: Be polite when speaking to your teacher. Use time phrases like 'after school', 'then', and 'before bed' to show the order of your plans.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises polite conversation with a teacher using 'be going to'. Sequencing words like 'after', 'then', and 'before' help you organise multiple future plans in a logical order.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are at a travel agency. The travel agent asks about your holiday plans. Answer the agent's questions using 'be going to'. Ask one question back to the agent using 'be going to' as well.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Welcome to Happy Travel Agency! I can help you plan your holiday. Where are you going to go? How long are you going to stay? Tell me about your plans!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are visiting a travel agency to plan a holiday trip to Bali. The travel agent wants to know your plans so they can help you. You plan to go to Bali next month, stay for five days, visit temples and beaches, and try surfing for the first time. You also want to ask the agent if the hotel is going to provide breakfast.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a customer at a travel agency. You are planning a holiday to Bali. You should answer the agent's questions politely and clearly using 'I'm going to' or 'We are going to'. You should also ask one question using 'Is the hotel going to...?'
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I'm going to go to Bali next month. I'm going to stay for five days. I'm going to visit temples and beaches, and I'm going to try surfing. Is the hotel going to provide breakfast?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ tə ˈbɑː.li nɛkst mʌnθ. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə steɪ fɔːr faɪv deɪz. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈvɪz.ɪt ˈtɛm.pəlz ænd ˈbiː.tʃɪz ænd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə traɪ ˈsɜːrf.ɪŋ. ɪz ðə hoʊˈtɛl ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə prəˈvaɪd ˈbrɛk.fəst/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember to also ask a question! Use 'Is the hotel going to...?' with rising intonation at the end. This shows you can use 'be going to' in questions too.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'be going to' in a real-world service situation. You practise both answering questions and asking questions using the target structure. The question form 'Is/Are + subject + going to + verb' is important at A1 level.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You are talking to your classmate about a group project. Discuss what each person in your group is going to do. Use 'be going to' with different subjects: I, you, he, she, we.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hey! We need to finish our group project by Friday. Let's talk about the plan. What is each person going to do? Tell me who is going to do what!
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your classmate are planning a group project about animals. There are four people in your group: you, your classmate (the person you are talking to), Rina, and Budi. You need to divide the work. You are going to write the report. Your classmate is going to make the poster. Rina is going to find pictures. Budi is going to present the project to the class.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student discussing a group project with your classmate. You are the group leader and you are telling everyone what they are going to do. Use different subjects with 'be going to': 'I'm going to', 'You are going to', 'She is going to', 'He is going to', 'We are going to'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I'm going to write the report. You are going to make the poster. Rina is going to find pictures. Budi is going to present the project. We are going to finish by Friday.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə raɪt ðə rɪˈpɔːrt. juː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə meɪk ðə ˈpoʊ.stər. ˈriː.nə ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə faɪnd ˈpɪk.tʃərz. ˈbuː.di ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə prɪˈzɛnt ðə ˈprɒdʒ.ɛkt. wiː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈfɪn.ɪʃ baɪ ˈfraɪ.deɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Change the subject for each sentence: I, you, she, he, we. Remember that 'he' and 'she' use 'is going to', while 'you' and 'we' use 'are going to'. This shows you can use all forms!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises 'be going to' with different subjects. At A1 level, learners must show they can conjugate 'be' correctly: I am, you are, he/she is, we are. Using all these forms in one conversation demonstrates good grammatical control.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing the vocabulary word 'intention' correctly. This word means a plan or purpose to do something in the future.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the word 'intention'. It means a plan you have decided to do.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My intention is to study English every day.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ ɪnˈtɛn.ʃən ɪz tə ˈstʌd.i ˈɪŋ.ɡlɪʃ ˈɛv.ri deɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: The word 'intention' has three syllables: in-TEN-tion. The stress is on the second syllable 'TEN'. The ending '-tion' sounds like /ʃən/. Do not say 'ten-see-on'.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The word 'intention' is a key vocabulary item in this unit about future plans. It is a noun that means 'a plan or purpose'. The pronunciation /ɪnˈtɛn.ʃən/ has stress on 'TEN' and the '-tion' suffix is pronounced /ʃən/, which is a common English pattern.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following three sentences out loud. Each sentence uses a different form of 'be going to': affirmative, negative, and question. Focus on correct grammar and clear delivery.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say these three sentences. Pay attention to the grammar: one is positive, one is negative, and one is a question. Make sure you use the correct form of 'be' with 'going to'.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: She is going to cook dinner. They are not going to play football. Are we going to watch a movie tonight?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ʃiː ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə kʊk ˈdɪn.ər. ðeɪ ɑːr nɒt ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl. ɑːr wiː ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə wɒtʃ ə ˈmuː.vi təˈnaɪt/
practicumQuestions.hint: For the negative, stress the word 'NOT' clearly: 'They are NOT going to play.' For the question, move 'are' to the front and use rising intonation at the end: 'ARE we going to watch...?' ↗
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises three forms of 'be going to': affirmative (She is going to cook), negative (They are not going to play), and interrogative (Are we going to watch?). Correct use of 'be' (is/are) and word order in questions is essential at A1 level.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following two words and notice how the stress changes. First say 'visit' alone, then say 'going to visit'. Pay attention to which syllables are strong and which are weak.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat. First word: VISIT. Now the phrase: GOING to VISIT. Notice that both 'GO' and 'VIS' are stressed, but 'to' is weak. Now say this full sentence: I'm GOING to VISIT my grandmother.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I'm going to visit my grandmother.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈvɪz.ɪt maɪ ˈɡrænd.mʌð.ər/
practicumQuestions.hint: In the phrase 'going to visit', there are two stressed syllables: 'GO' and 'VIS'. The word 'to' between them is very short and weak: /tə/. This creates a rhythm: STRONG-weak-weak-STRONG-weak. Tap your hand on the stressed syllables to feel the beat.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill focuses on syllable stress patterns in 'be going to + verb' phrases. English has a stress-timed rhythm, meaning stressed syllables come at regular intervals. The weak 'to' /tə/ between two stressed words creates the natural English rhythm that A1 learners need to develop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say the following two sentences. The first is a statement — use falling intonation. The second is a yes/no question — use rising intonation. Feel the difference in your voice at the end of each sentence.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say these two sentences. For the first sentence, let your voice go DOWN at the end because it is a statement. For the second sentence, let your voice go UP at the end because it is a yes/no question. Ready? Go!
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I'm going to study tonight. Are you going to study tonight?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈstʌd.i təˈnaɪt ↘ ɑːr juː ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈstʌd.i təˈnaɪt ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: Statement: 'I'm going to study toNIGHT.' ↘ Your voice falls on 'tonight'. Question: 'Are you going to study toNIGHT?' ↗ Your voice rises on 'tonight'. The words are almost the same, but the intonation changes the meaning completely!
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill contrasts falling intonation (for statements about plans) and rising intonation (for yes/no questions about plans). In English, intonation carries meaning: falling tone = giving information, rising tone = asking for confirmation. Both sentences use 'be going to' but the intonation pattern tells the listener whether you are stating a plan or asking about one.

reading.question: According to the passage, where does Rina's grandmother live?
options: In a small town near the mountains.
In a big city near the beach.
In the same town as Rina.
reading.answer: In a small town near the mountains.
reading.explanation: Rina says, 'She lives in a small town near the mountains.' This detail is stated directly in the passage. Always scan the text for specific location words!

reading.question: Which sentence from the passage uses the NEGATIVE form of 'be going to'?
options: I'm not going to play video games this weekend.
I'm going to study for my English test.
We're going to have a picnic.
reading.answer: I'm not going to play video games this weekend.
reading.explanation: The negative form uses 'not' between 'am/is/are' and 'going to.' Tom says 'I'm not going to play video games,' which shows a decision NOT to do something. The other two sentences are affirmative (positive) plans.

reading.question: When Rina asks, 'Are you going to study all day?' — what does Tom answer?
options: No, I'm not. He is going to take a break in the evening.
Yes, I am. He is going to study all day and all night.
He doesn't answer the question.
reading.answer: No, I'm not. He is going to take a break in the evening.
reading.explanation: Tom replies, 'No, I'm not. I'm going to take a break in the evening.' This shows how to answer a 'be going to' question with a short negative answer and then give more details about the plan.

reading.question: Read this sentence: 'We're going to have a picnic.' Who says this in the passage?
options: Maya, talking about her plan with her cousins.
Rina, talking about her plan with her grandmother.
Tom, talking about his plan with his friends.
reading.answer: Maya, talking about her plan with her cousins.
reading.explanation: Maya says, 'I'm going to meet my cousins at the park on Saturday. We're going to have a picnic.' The word 'we' refers to Maya and her cousins. Scanning for who is speaking helps you understand the details!

reading.question: Which of these is the correct structure for 'be going to' in a question?
options: Are you going to study tonight?
You are going to study tonight?
Going to are you study tonight?
reading.answer: Are you going to study tonight?
reading.explanation: To form a question with 'be going to,' we move the 'be' verb (am/is/are) to the front: 'Are + you + going to + study + tonight?' This is the correct word order for yes/no questions.

reading.question: At the end of the passage, Maya says, 'We are all going to have a great weekend!' What does this sentence express?
options: A positive feeling about everyone's future plans.
A question about what everyone did last weekend.
A complaint that the weekend is too busy.
reading.answer: A positive feeling about everyone's future plans.
reading.explanation: Maya uses 'be going to' to express a happy, confident feeling about the future. The word 'great' shows it is positive. She is not asking a question or complaining — she is sharing her excitement about everyone's plans!

reading.question: Look at this sentence from the passage: 'I'm going to cook lunch for her.' What form is the verb 'cook' in?
options: Base form (infinitive) — the simple, unchanged form of the verb.
Past tense — the verb shows a completed action.
Present continuous (-ing form) — the verb shows an action happening now.
reading.answer: Base form (infinitive) — the simple, unchanged form of the verb.
reading.explanation: After 'going to,' we always use the base form of the verb. 'Cook' is the base form. We do NOT say 'going to cooks,' 'going to cooked,' or 'going to cooking.' This is an important rule to remember!

Childs

reading.question: What is the weather like when it is raining?

Dry
Sunny
reading.explanation: Rain brings water, making the weather and ground wet.

reading.question: Choose the correct form: 'They _____ playing football right now.'
options: are
is
am
reading.explanation: 'They' requires the plural auxiliary 'are' in present continuous.

reading.question: What is Jamie's nationality?
options: Spanish
French
Italian
reading.explanation: Jamie is from Spain, so his nationality is Spanish.

reading.question: Which sentence is the correct negative form of 'She likes coffee'?
options: She doesn't like coffee.
She not likes coffee.
She don't like coffee.
reading.explanation: For third person singular (she/he/it), we use 'doesn't + base verb'.

reading.question: Where do they usually eat dinner on weekdays?
options: At home with family
In a luxury restaurant
At the airport
reading.explanation: Daily routines typically describe having dinner at home with family.

reading.question: What time does the train to London depart?
options: At 8:30 in the morning
At midnight
Next week
reading.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

reading.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday, we _____ a new car.'
options: bought
buyed
buying
reading.explanation: 'Buy' is an irregular verb whose past simple form is 'bought'.

writing.prompt: Write three sentences about what you are going to do after school today. Use 'am going to' in each sentence. Include a time word in at least one sentence.
writing.criteria: Each sentence uses 'I am going to + base verb' correctly. At least one sentence has a time expression (e.g., 'today', 'tonight', 'this afternoon'). All sentences start with a capital letter and end with a period. Spelling of common words is correct.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: I am going to eat lunch with my friends today. I am going to do my homework at home. I am going to read a book tonight.

writing.prompt: Write two negative sentences and one question about future plans. Use 'is not going to' or 'are not going to' for the negative sentences. Use 'Is' or 'Are' to start the question.
writing.criteria: Negative sentences correctly use 'subject + is/are + not + going to + base verb'. The question uses correct word order: 'Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + base verb?' All sentences have correct capitalization and punctuation. The main verb after 'going to' is in base form.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: Tom is not going to play video games tonight. We are not going to eat fast food tomorrow. Is she going to visit the museum next week?

writing.prompt: Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) about your plans for next year. Include at least two positive sentences with 'going to', one negative sentence with 'not going to', and one question. Use different subjects (I, he, she, we, they).
writing.criteria: The paragraph has 4 to 6 sentences. It includes at least two positive 'be going to' sentences, one negative 'be going to' sentence, and one question with 'be going to'. Different subjects are used (not only 'I'). Correct subject-verb agreement with am/is/are. All sentences have proper capitalization and end punctuation. Time expressions related to the future are present.
writing.sampleGoodAnswer: Next year, I am going to learn how to swim. My sister is going to start university. We are going to move to a new house. My brother is not going to change his school. Are they going to visit us next summer? I am going to work very hard.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about your plans for next weekend. Use 'be going to' for each plan. Follow the three story points below. Speak clearly with falling intonation for each statement.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me about your plans for next weekend. What are you going to do? Where are you going to go? Who are you going to be with? Use 'I'm going to' in your story.
storyPoints: Say where you are going to go next weekend and why.
Say what activity you are going to do there.
Say who you are going to go with and how you are going to travel.
speaking.targetSentence: Next weekend, I'm going to go to the beach because I love the sea. I'm going to swim and play in the sand. I'm going to go with my friends, and we are going to travel by car.
speaking.phonetic: /nɛkst ˈwiːk.ɛnd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ tə ðə biːtʃ bɪˈkɒz aɪ lʌv ðə siː. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə swɪm ænd pleɪ ɪn ðə sænd. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ wɪð maɪ frɛndz ænd wiː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈtræv.əl baɪ kɑːr/
speaking.hint: Remember to use 'I'm going to' before each verb. Speak slowly and clearly. Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence.
speaking.explanation: This storytelling task practises using 'be going to' to describe future plans in a connected monologue. You should use the structure 'subject + be going to + base verb' for each plan. Falling intonation at the end of each statement shows confidence.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about your plans for the school holiday. Use 'be going to' to describe three different plans. Follow the story points below and speak with clear pronunciation.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please tell me about your school holiday plans. What are you going to do during the holiday? Tell me about three things you are going to do. Use 'I'm going to' or 'We are going to' in your story.
storyPoints: Say what you are going to do in the first week of the holiday.
Say what food you are going to try or cook.
Say what you are NOT going to do during the holiday and why.
speaking.targetSentence: In the first week, I'm going to visit my grandparents in the village. I'm going to try my grandmother's special fried rice. I'm not going to study every day because I want to relax and have fun.
speaking.phonetic: /ɪn ðə fɜːrst wiːk aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈvɪz.ɪt maɪ ˈɡrænd.pɛr.ənts ɪn ðə ˈvɪl.ɪdʒ. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə traɪ maɪ ˈɡrænd.mʌð.ərz ˈspɛʃ.əl fraɪd raɪs. aɪm nɒt ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈstʌd.i ˈɛv.ri deɪ bɪˈkɒz aɪ wɒnt tə rɪˈlæks ænd hæv fʌn/
speaking.hint: Include one negative sentence using 'I'm NOT going to'. Stress the word 'NOT' clearly. Remember to follow all three story points.
speaking.explanation: This task practises both affirmative and negative forms of 'be going to'. Using 'I'm not going to' is important for expressing things you do not plan to do. The three story points guide you to create a structured monologue.

speaking.instruction: You are calling your friend to talk about your plans for tomorrow. Your friend will ask you questions about your plans. Answer using 'I'm going to + verb'. Be friendly and speak clearly.

speaking.scenarioContext: You are having a phone call with your friend. Tomorrow is Saturday and you have no school. Your friend wants to know your plans. You have planned to go shopping at the mall, eat lunch at a restaurant, and watch a movie in the evening. Use 'I'm going to' to tell your friend about each plan.
speaking.characterRole: You are a student talking to your friend on the phone. You are excited about your plans for tomorrow. You should answer questions about where you are going to go, what you are going to eat, and what you are going to do in the evening.
speaking.targetSentence: I'm going to go shopping at the mall. Then I'm going to eat lunch at a restaurant. In the evening, I'm going to watch a movie.
speaking.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ ˈʃɒp.ɪŋ æt ðə mɔːl. ðɛn aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə iːt lʌntʃ æt ə ˈrɛs.tər.ɒnt. ɪn ðə ˈiːv.nɪŋ aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə wɒtʃ ə ˈmuː.vi/
speaking.hint: Use time words like 'then' and 'in the evening' to organise your plans. Speak with enthusiasm because you are excited about tomorrow!
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'be going to' in a natural phone conversation. You need to respond to your friend's questions with clear plans using the target structure. Using time markers helps organise your ideas.

speaking.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, about your plans after you finish school today. He will ask you several questions. Answer each question using 'be going to'.

speaking.scenarioContext: You are in the classroom after the last lesson. Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, wants to practise English conversation with you. He asks about your plans for this afternoon. You plan to go home, do your homework, help your mother cook dinner, and then read a book before bed.
speaking.characterRole: You are a student speaking to your English teacher Mr. Khoirul. You should be polite and answer in complete sentences using 'I'm going to'. You are a responsible student who has clear plans for the afternoon.
speaking.targetSentence: After school, I'm going to go home and do my homework. Then I'm going to help my mother cook dinner. Before bed, I'm going to read a book.
speaking.phonetic: /ˈæf.tər skuːl aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ hoʊm ænd duː maɪ ˈhoʊm.wɜːrk. ðɛn aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə hɛlp maɪ ˈmʌð.ər kʊk ˈdɪn.ər. bɪˈfɔːr bɛd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə riːd ə bʊk/
speaking.hint: Be polite when speaking to your teacher. Use time phrases like 'after school', 'then', and 'before bed' to show the order of your plans.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises polite conversation with a teacher using 'be going to'. Sequencing words like 'after', 'then', and 'before' help you organise multiple future plans in a logical order.

speaking.instruction: You are at a travel agency. The travel agent asks about your holiday plans. Answer the agent's questions using 'be going to'. Ask one question back to the agent using 'be going to' as well.
speaking.audioPrompt: Welcome to Happy Travel Agency! I can help you plan your holiday. Where are you going to go? How long are you going to stay? Tell me about your plans!
speaking.scenarioContext: You are visiting a travel agency to plan a holiday trip to Bali. The travel agent wants to know your plans so they can help you. You plan to go to Bali next month, stay for five days, visit temples and beaches, and try surfing for the first time. You also want to ask the agent if the hotel is going to provide breakfast.
speaking.characterRole: You are a customer at a travel agency. You are planning a holiday to Bali. You should answer the agent's questions politely and clearly using 'I'm going to' or 'We are going to'. You should also ask one question using 'Is the hotel going to...?'
speaking.targetSentence: I'm going to go to Bali next month. I'm going to stay for five days. I'm going to visit temples and beaches, and I'm going to try surfing. Is the hotel going to provide breakfast?
speaking.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ tə ˈbɑː.li nɛkst mʌnθ. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə steɪ fɔːr faɪv deɪz. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈvɪz.ɪt ˈtɛm.pəlz ænd ˈbiː.tʃɪz ænd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə traɪ ˈsɜːrf.ɪŋ. ɪz ðə hoʊˈtɛl ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə prəˈvaɪd ˈbrɛk.fəst/
speaking.hint: Remember to also ask a question! Use 'Is the hotel going to...?' with rising intonation at the end. This shows you can use 'be going to' in questions too.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'be going to' in a real-world service situation. You practise both answering questions and asking questions using the target structure. The question form 'Is/Are + subject + going to + verb' is important at A1 level.

speaking.instruction: You are talking to your classmate about a group project. Discuss what each person in your group is going to do. Use 'be going to' with different subjects: I, you, he, she, we.
speaking.audioPrompt: Hey! We need to finish our group project by Friday. Let's talk about the plan. What is each person going to do? Tell me who is going to do what!
speaking.scenarioContext: You and your classmate are planning a group project about animals. There are four people in your group: you, your classmate (the person you are talking to), Rina, and Budi. You need to divide the work. You are going to write the report. Your classmate is going to make the poster. Rina is going to find pictures. Budi is going to present the project to the class.
speaking.characterRole: You are a student discussing a group project with your classmate. You are the group leader and you are telling everyone what they are going to do. Use different subjects with 'be going to': 'I'm going to', 'You are going to', 'She is going to', 'He is going to', 'We are going to'.
speaking.targetSentence: I'm going to write the report. You are going to make the poster. Rina is going to find pictures. Budi is going to present the project. We are going to finish by Friday.
speaking.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə raɪt ðə rɪˈpɔːrt. juː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə meɪk ðə ˈpoʊ.stər. ˈriː.nə ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə faɪnd ˈpɪk.tʃərz. ˈbuː.di ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə prɪˈzɛnt ðə ˈprɒdʒ.ɛkt. wiː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈfɪn.ɪʃ baɪ ˈfraɪ.deɪ/
speaking.hint: Change the subject for each sentence: I, you, she, he, we. Remember that 'he' and 'she' use 'is going to', while 'you' and 'we' use 'are going to'. This shows you can use all forms!
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises 'be going to' with different subjects. At A1 level, learners must show they can conjugate 'be' correctly: I am, you are, he/she is, we are. Using all these forms in one conversation demonstrates good grammatical control.

speaking.instruction: Say the following sentence out loud. Focus on pronouncing the vocabulary word 'intention' correctly. This word means a plan or purpose to do something in the future.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please say this sentence clearly. Pay attention to the word 'intention'. It means a plan you have decided to do.
speaking.targetSentence: My intention is to study English every day.
speaking.phonetic: /maɪ ɪnˈtɛn.ʃən ɪz tə ˈstʌd.i ˈɪŋ.ɡlɪʃ ˈɛv.ri deɪ/
speaking.hint: The word 'intention' has three syllables: in-TEN-tion. The stress is on the second syllable 'TEN'. The ending '-tion' sounds like /ʃən/. Do not say 'ten-see-on'.
speaking.explanation: The word 'intention' is a key vocabulary item in this unit about future plans. It is a noun that means 'a plan or purpose'. The pronunciation /ɪnˈtɛn.ʃən/ has stress on 'TEN' and the '-tion' suffix is pronounced /ʃən/, which is a common English pattern.

speaking.instruction: Say the following three sentences out loud. Each sentence uses a different form of 'be going to': affirmative, negative, and question. Focus on correct grammar and clear delivery.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please say these three sentences. Pay attention to the grammar: one is positive, one is negative, and one is a question. Make sure you use the correct form of 'be' with 'going to'.
speaking.targetSentence: She is going to cook dinner. They are not going to play football. Are we going to watch a movie tonight?
speaking.phonetic: /ʃiː ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə kʊk ˈdɪn.ər. ðeɪ ɑːr nɒt ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə pleɪ ˈfʊt.bɔːl. ɑːr wiː ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə wɒtʃ ə ˈmuː.vi təˈnaɪt/
speaking.hint: For the negative, stress the word 'NOT' clearly: 'They are NOT going to play.' For the question, move 'are' to the front and use rising intonation at the end: 'ARE we going to watch...?' ↗
speaking.explanation: This drill practises three forms of 'be going to': affirmative (She is going to cook), negative (They are not going to play), and interrogative (Are we going to watch?). Correct use of 'be' (is/are) and word order in questions is essential at A1 level.

speaking.instruction: Say the following two words and notice how the stress changes. First say 'visit' alone, then say 'going to visit'. Pay attention to which syllables are strong and which are weak.
speaking.audioPrompt: Listen and repeat. First word: VISIT. Now the phrase: GOING to VISIT. Notice that both 'GO' and 'VIS' are stressed, but 'to' is weak. Now say this full sentence: I'm GOING to VISIT my grandmother.
speaking.targetSentence: I'm going to visit my grandmother.
speaking.hint: In the phrase 'going to visit', there are two stressed syllables: 'GO' and 'VIS'. The word 'to' between them is very short and weak: /tə/. This creates a rhythm: STRONG-weak-weak-STRONG-weak. Tap your hand on the stressed syllables to feel the beat.
speaking.explanation: This drill focuses on syllable stress patterns in 'be going to + verb' phrases. English has a stress-timed rhythm, meaning stressed syllables come at regular intervals. The weak 'to' /tə/ between two stressed words creates the natural English rhythm that A1 learners need to develop.

speaking.instruction: Say the following two sentences. The first is a statement — use falling intonation. The second is a yes/no question — use rising intonation. Feel the difference in your voice at the end of each sentence.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please say these two sentences. For the first sentence, let your voice go DOWN at the end because it is a statement. For the second sentence, let your voice go UP at the end because it is a yes/no question. Ready? Go!
speaking.targetSentence: I'm going to study tonight. Are you going to study tonight?
speaking.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈstʌd.i təˈnaɪt ↘ ɑːr juː ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈstʌd.i təˈnaɪt ↗/
speaking.hint: Statement: 'I'm going to study toNIGHT.' ↘ Your voice falls on 'tonight'. Question: 'Are you going to study toNIGHT?' ↗ Your voice rises on 'tonight'. The words are almost the same, but the intonation changes the meaning completely!
speaking.explanation: This drill contrasts falling intonation (for statements about plans) and rising intonation (for yes/no questions about plans). In English, intonation carries meaning: falling tone = giving information, rising tone = asking for confirmation. Both sentences use 'be going to' but the intonation pattern tells the listener whether you are stating a plan or asking about one.

questions.question: According to the passage, where does Rina's grandmother live?
options: In a small town near the mountains.
In a big city near the beach.
In the same town as Rina.
questions.answer: In a small town near the mountains.
questions.explanation: Rina says, 'She lives in a small town near the mountains.' This detail is stated directly in the passage. Always scan the text for specific location words!

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage uses the NEGATIVE form of 'be going to'?
options: I'm not going to play video games this weekend.
I'm going to study for my English test.
We're going to have a picnic.
questions.answer: I'm not going to play video games this weekend.
questions.explanation: The negative form uses 'not' between 'am/is/are' and 'going to.' Tom says 'I'm not going to play video games,' which shows a decision NOT to do something. The other two sentences are affirmative (positive) plans.

questions.question: When Rina asks, 'Are you going to study all day?' — what does Tom answer?
options: No, I'm not. He is going to take a break in the evening.
Yes, I am. He is going to study all day and all night.
He doesn't answer the question.
questions.answer: No, I'm not. He is going to take a break in the evening.
questions.explanation: Tom replies, 'No, I'm not. I'm going to take a break in the evening.' This shows how to answer a 'be going to' question with a short negative answer and then give more details about the plan.

questions.question: Read this sentence: 'We're going to have a picnic.' Who says this in the passage?
options: Maya, talking about her plan with her cousins.
Rina, talking about her plan with her grandmother.
Tom, talking about his plan with his friends.
questions.answer: Maya, talking about her plan with her cousins.
questions.explanation: Maya says, 'I'm going to meet my cousins at the park on Saturday. We're going to have a picnic.' The word 'we' refers to Maya and her cousins. Scanning for who is speaking helps you understand the details!

questions.question: Which of these is the correct structure for 'be going to' in a question?
options: Are you going to study tonight?
You are going to study tonight?
Going to are you study tonight?
questions.answer: Are you going to study tonight?
questions.explanation: To form a question with 'be going to,' we move the 'be' verb (am/is/are) to the front: 'Are + you + going to + study + tonight?' This is the correct word order for yes/no questions.

questions.question: At the end of the passage, Maya says, 'We are all going to have a great weekend!' What does this sentence express?
options: A positive feeling about everyone's future plans.
A question about what everyone did last weekend.
A complaint that the weekend is too busy.
questions.answer: A positive feeling about everyone's future plans.
questions.explanation: Maya uses 'be going to' to express a happy, confident feeling about the future. The word 'great' shows it is positive. She is not asking a question or complaining — she is sharing her excitement about everyone's plans!

questions.question: Look at this sentence from the passage: 'I'm going to cook lunch for her.' What form is the verb 'cook' in?
options: Base form (infinitive) — the simple, unchanged form of the verb.
Past tense — the verb shows a completed action.
Present continuous (-ing form) — the verb shows an action happening now.
questions.answer: Base form (infinitive) — the simple, unchanged form of the verb.
questions.explanation: After 'going to,' we always use the base form of the verb. 'Cook' is the base form. We do NOT say 'going to cooks,' 'going to cooked,' or 'going to cooking.' This is an important rule to remember!

questions.question: Which plural form is correct?
options: Children
Childs
Childrens
questions.answer: Children
questions.explanation: 'Child' has the irregular plural form 'children'.

questions.question: What is the weather like when it is raining?
options: Wet
Dry
Sunny
questions.answer: Wet
questions.explanation: Rain brings water, making the weather and ground wet.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'They _____ playing football right now.'
options: are
is
am
questions.answer: are
questions.explanation: 'They' requires the plural auxiliary 'are' in present continuous.

questions.question: What is Jamie's nationality?

questions.explanation: Jamie is from Spain, so his nationality is Spanish.

questions.question: Which sentence is the correct negative form of 'She likes coffee'?
options: She doesn't like coffee.
She not likes coffee.
She don't like coffee.
questions.answer: She doesn't like coffee.
questions.explanation: For third person singular (she/he/it), we use 'doesn't + base verb'.

questions.question: Where do they usually eat dinner on weekdays?

In a luxury restaurant

questions.explanation: Daily routines typically describe having dinner at home with family.

questions.question: What time does the train to London depart?

At midnight
Next week

questions.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

questions.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday, we _____ a new car.'

buyed

questions.answer: bought
questions.explanation: 'Buy' is an irregular verb whose past simple form is 'bought'.

questions.prompt: Write three sentences about what you are going to do after school today. Use 'am going to' in each sentence. Include a time word in at least one sentence.
questions.criteria: Each sentence uses 'I am going to + base verb' correctly. At least one sentence has a time expression (e.g., 'today', 'tonight', 'this afternoon'). All sentences start with a capital letter and end with a period. Spelling of common words is correct.
questions.sampleGoodAnswer: I am going to eat lunch with my friends today. I am going to do my homework at home. I am going to read a book tonight.

questions.prompt: Write two negative sentences and one question about future plans. Use 'is not going to' or 'are not going to' for the negative sentences. Use 'Is' or 'Are' to start the question.
questions.criteria: Negative sentences correctly use 'subject + is/are + not + going to + base verb'. The question uses correct word order: 'Am/Is/Are + subject + going to + base verb?' All sentences have correct capitalization and punctuation. The main verb after 'going to' is in base form.
questions.sampleGoodAnswer: Tom is not going to play video games tonight. We are not going to eat fast food tomorrow. Is she going to visit the museum next week?

questions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (4 to 6 sentences) about your plans for next year. Include at least two positive sentences with 'going to', one negative sentence with 'not going to', and one question. Use different subjects (I, he, she, we, they).
questions.criteria: The paragraph has 4 to 6 sentences. It includes at least two positive 'be going to' sentences, one negative 'be going to' sentence, and one question with 'be going to'. Different subjects are used (not only 'I'). Correct subject-verb agreement with am/is/are. All sentences have proper capitalization and end punctuation. Time expressions related to the future are present.
questions.sampleGoodAnswer: Next year, I am going to learn how to swim. My sister is going to start university. We are going to move to a new house. My brother is not going to change his school. Are they going to visit us next summer? I am going to work very hard.

questions.instruction: Tell a short story about your plans for next weekend. Use 'be going to' for each plan. Follow the three story points below. Speak clearly with falling intonation for each statement.
questions.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me about your plans for next weekend. What are you going to do? Where are you going to go? Who are you going to be with? Use 'I'm going to' in your story.
storyPoints: Say where you are going to go next weekend and why.
Say what activity you are going to do there.
Say who you are going to go with and how you are going to travel.
questions.targetSentence: Next weekend, I'm going to go to the beach because I love the sea. I'm going to swim and play in the sand. I'm going to go with my friends, and we are going to travel by car.
questions.phonetic: /nɛkst ˈwiːk.ɛnd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ tə ðə biːtʃ bɪˈkɒz aɪ lʌv ðə siː. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə swɪm ænd pleɪ ɪn ðə sænd. aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ wɪð maɪ frɛndz ænd wiː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈtræv.əl baɪ kɑːr/
questions.hint: Remember to use 'I'm going to' before each verb. Speak slowly and clearly. Let your voice fall at the end of each sentence.
questions.explanation: This storytelling task practises using 'be going to' to describe future plans in a connected monologue. You should use the structure 'subject + be going to + base verb' for each plan. Falling intonation at the end of each statement shows confidence.

questions.instruction: Tell a short story about your plans for the school holiday. Use 'be going to' to describe three different plans. Follow the story points below and speak with clear pronunciation.

storyPoints: Say what you are going to do in the first week of the holiday.
Say what food you are going to try or cook.
Say what you are NOT going to do during the holiday and why.

questions.hint: Include one negative sentence using 'I'm NOT going to'. Stress the word 'NOT' clearly. Remember to follow all three story points.
questions.explanation: This task practises both affirmative and negative forms of 'be going to'. Using 'I'm not going to' is important for expressing things you do not plan to do. The three story points guide you to create a structured monologue.

questions.instruction: You are calling your friend to talk about your plans for tomorrow. Your friend will ask you questions about your plans. Answer using 'I'm going to + verb'. Be friendly and speak clearly.
questions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is your friend calling. I want to know about your plans for tomorrow. Let's talk about what you are going to do!
questions.scenarioContext: You are having a phone call with your friend. Tomorrow is Saturday and you have no school. Your friend wants to know your plans. You have planned to go shopping at the mall, eat lunch at a restaurant, and watch a movie in the evening. Use 'I'm going to' to tell your friend about each plan.
questions.characterRole: You are a student talking to your friend on the phone. You are excited about your plans for tomorrow. You should answer questions about where you are going to go, what you are going to eat, and what you are going to do in the evening.
questions.targetSentence: I'm going to go shopping at the mall. Then I'm going to eat lunch at a restaurant. In the evening, I'm going to watch a movie.
questions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ ˈʃɒp.ɪŋ æt ðə mɔːl. ðɛn aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə iːt lʌntʃ æt ə ˈrɛs.tər.ɒnt. ɪn ðə ˈiːv.nɪŋ aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə wɒtʃ ə ˈmuː.vi/
questions.hint: Use time words like 'then' and 'in the evening' to organise your plans. Speak with enthusiasm because you are excited about tomorrow!
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'be going to' in a natural phone conversation. You need to respond to your friend's questions with clear plans using the target structure. Using time markers helps organise your ideas.

questions.instruction: You are talking to Mr. Khoirul, your English teacher, about your plans after you finish school today. He will ask you several questions. Answer each question using 'be going to'.

questions.characterRole: You are a student speaking to your English teacher Mr. Khoirul. You should be polite and answer in complete sentences using 'I'm going to'. You are a responsible student who has clear plans for the afternoon.
questions.targetSentence: After school, I'm going to go home and do my homework. Then I'm going to help my mother cook dinner. Before bed, I'm going to read a book.
questions.phonetic: /ˈæf.tər skuːl aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ɡoʊ hoʊm ænd duː maɪ ˈhoʊm.wɜːrk. ðɛn aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə hɛlp maɪ ˈmʌð.ər kʊk ˈdɪn.ər. bɪˈfɔːr bɛd aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə riːd ə bʊk/
questions.hint: Be polite when speaking to your teacher. Use time phrases like 'after school', 'then', and 'before bed' to show the order of your plans.
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises polite conversation with a teacher using 'be going to'. Sequencing words like 'after', 'then', and 'before' help you organise multiple future plans in a logical order.

questions.instruction: You are at a travel agency. The travel agent asks about your holiday plans. Answer the agent's questions using 'be going to'. Ask one question back to the agent using 'be going to' as well.
questions.audioPrompt: Welcome to Happy Travel Agency! I can help you plan your holiday. Where are you going to go? How long are you going to stay? Tell me about your plans!
questions.scenarioContext: You are visiting a travel agency to plan a holiday trip to Bali. The travel agent wants to know your plans so they can help you. You plan to go to Bali next month, stay for five days, visit temples and beaches, and try surfing for the first time. You also want to ask the agent if the hotel is going to provide breakfast.
questions.characterRole: You are a customer at a travel agency. You are planning a holiday to Bali. You should answer the agent's questions politely and clearly using 'I'm going to' or 'We are going to'. You should also ask one question using 'Is the hotel going to...?'
questions.targetSentence: I'm going to go to Bali next month. I'm going to stay for five days. I'm going to visit temples and beaches, and I'm going to try surfing. Is the hotel going to provide breakfast?

questions.hint: Remember to also ask a question! Use 'Is the hotel going to...?' with rising intonation at the end. This shows you can use 'be going to' in questions too.
questions.explanation: This roleplay practises using 'be going to' in a real-world service situation. You practise both answering questions and asking questions using the target structure. The question form 'Is/Are + subject + going to + verb' is important at A1 level.

questions.instruction: You are talking to your classmate about a group project. Discuss what each person in your group is going to do. Use 'be going to' with different subjects: I, you, he, she, we.
questions.audioPrompt: Hey! We need to finish our group project by Friday. Let's talk about the plan. What is each person going to do? Tell me who is going to do what!

You need to divide the work. You are going to write the report. Your classmate is going to make the poster. Rina is going to find pictures. Budi is going to present the project to the class.
questions.characterRole: You are a student discussing a group project with your classmate. You are the group leader and you are telling everyone what they are going to do. Use different subjects with 'be going to': 'I'm going to', 'You are going to', 'She is going to', 'He is going to', 'We are going to'.
questions.targetSentence: I'm going to write the report. You are going to make the poster. Rina is going to find pictures. Budi is going to present the project. We are going to finish by Friday.
questions.phonetic: /aɪm ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə raɪt ðə rɪˈpɔːrt. juː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə meɪk ðə ˈpoʊ.stər. ˈriː.nə ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə faɪnd ˈpɪk.tʃərz. ˈbuː.di ɪz ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə prɪˈzɛnt ðə ˈprɒdʒ.ɛkt. wiː ɑːr ˈɡoʊ.ɪŋ tə ˈfɪn.ɪʃ baɪ ˈfraɪ.deɪ/
